```{ojs}
//| echo: false
huOrder = (q, n) => {
  let h = 0;
  for (const ch of q) h = (h * 31 + ch.charCodeAt(0)) >>> 0;
  return d3.shuffler(d3.randomLcg((h % 10000) / 10000))(d3.range(n));
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
huBuildCards = function(body, questions, onAnswer) {
  questions.forEach((qq, qi) => {
    const card = document.createElement("div");
    card.className = "hu-qcard";
    card.style.cssText = "background:#fff;color:#1e1b4b;border-radius:12px;padding:16px 18px;margin-bottom:14px;box-shadow:0 2px 8px rgba(0,0,0,.1);border:1px solid #e2e8f0;";
    card.innerHTML = `<p style="font-weight:700;margin:0 0 10px;color:#1e1b4b;">${qi+1}. ${qq.q}</p>`;
    const fb = document.createElement("div");
    fb.style.cssText = "border-radius:8px;font-size:.9em;";
    const order = huOrder(qq.q, qq.options.length);
    const shownCorrect = order.indexOf(qq.correct);
    order.map(i => qq.options[i]).forEach((opt, oi) => {
      const btn = document.createElement("button");
      btn.textContent = opt;
      btn.style.cssText = "display:block;width:100%;min-height:44px;text-align:left;padding:10px 14px;margin:6px 0;border:2px solid #e2e8f0;border-radius:8px;background:#fff;color:#1e1b4b;cursor:pointer;font-size:.95em;";
      btn.onclick = () => {
        if (card.dataset.answered) return;
        card.dataset.answered = "true";
        card.querySelectorAll("button").forEach(b => { b.style.cursor = "default"; });
        const right = card.querySelectorAll("button")[shownCorrect];
        right.style.borderColor = "#48bb78"; right.style.background = "#f0fff4"; right.style.color = "#22543d"; right.style.fontWeight = "700";
        const ok = oi === shownCorrect;
        if (ok) {
          fb.innerHTML = "✅ Correct! " + qq.explanation; fb.style.color = "#276749"; fb.style.background = "#f0fff4";
        } else {
          btn.style.borderColor = "#fc8181"; btn.style.background = "#fff5f5"; btn.style.color = "#9b2c2c";
          fb.innerHTML = "❌ Not quite. " + qq.explanation; fb.style.color = "#9b2c2c"; fb.style.background = "#fff5f5";
        }
        fb.style.padding = "10px 14px"; fb.style.marginTop = "8px";
        if (onAnswer) onAnswer(ok);
      };
      card.appendChild(btn);
    });
    card.appendChild(fb);
    body.appendChild(card);
  });
}
```

//| echo: false
huQuiz = function(id, title, questions) {
  const outer = html`<div id="${id}" style="margin:18px 0 24px 0;text-align:center;">
    <button class="hu-toggle" style="display:inline-flex;align-items:center;gap:7px;background:linear-gradient(135deg,#0284c7 0%,#4834a8 100%);color:#fff;border:none;padding:9px 22px;border-radius:50px;font-size:.95em;font-weight:700;cursor:pointer;min-height:44px;box-shadow:0 3px 12px rgba(2,132,199,.4);">
      <span style="font-size:1.1em;">📝</span> ${title}
      <span class="chevron" style="transition:transform .3s;">▼</span>
    </button>
    <div class="quiz-body" style="max-height:0;opacity:0;overflow:hidden;transition:max-height .5s cubic-bezier(.4,0,.2,1),opacity .4s ease,margin-top .3s ease;margin-top:0;text-align:left;">
      <button class="close-btn" style="display:block;margin:0 auto 10px auto;background:rgba(2,132,199,.12);color:#0369a1;border:none;padding:5px 18px;border-radius:50px;font-size:.85em;font-weight:600;cursor:pointer;min-height:36px;">Hide Quiz</button>
      <p style="text-align:center;color:#64748b;font-style:italic;font-size:.9em;margin-bottom:12px;">Select an answer for each question.</p>
    </div>
  </div>`;
  const toggle = outer.querySelector("button.hu-toggle");
  const chevron = toggle.querySelector(".chevron");
  const body = outer.querySelector(".quiz-body");
  const closeBtn = body.querySelector(".close-btn");
  function expand(){ body.style.maxHeight="5000px"; body.style.opacity="1"; body.style.marginTop="14px"; chevron.style.transform="rotate(180deg)"; }
  function collapse(){ body.style.maxHeight="0"; body.style.opacity="0"; body.style.marginTop="0"; chevron.style.transform="rotate(0)"; }
  toggle.onclick = () => body.style.maxHeight === "0px" || body.style.maxHeight === "" ? expand() : collapse();
  closeBtn.onclick = collapse;
  huBuildCards(body, questions);
  return outer;
}

  {name: "South Indian", season: "October–May", months: [9,10,11,0,1,2,3,4], avg: 6, hemi: "Southern",
   box: [[30, -30], [115, -5]], label: [72, -35]}

huMonths = ["Jan","Feb","Mar","Apr","May","Jun","Jul","Aug","Sep","Oct","Nov","Dec"]
huRing = ([[x0, y0], [x1, y1]]) => {
  const pts = [];
  for (let x = x0; x <= x1; x += 2) pts.push([x, y0]);
  for (let y = y0; y <= y1; y += 2) pts.push([x1, y]);
  for (let x = x1; x >= x0; x -= 2) pts.push([x, y1]);
  for (let y = y1; y >= y0; y -= 2) pts.push([x0, y]);
  pts.push([x0, y0]);
  return pts;
}
huProj = ({type: "equirectangular", rotate: [-180, 0],
  domain: {type: "MultiPoint", coordinates: [[0.5, -42], [90, -42], [180, -42], [270, -42], [359.5, -42], [0.5, 54], [90, 54], [180, 54], [270, 54], [359.5, 54]]}})
huHemiColor = ({Northern: "#0284c7", Southern: "#e11d48"})
```

# Engage: What do students know about hurricanes? {#hu-engage}

::: {.engage-box}
## 🌀 The 2005 Atlantic Hurricane Season

In the [Blizzards](unit5-blizzards.qmd) and [Paths of Severe Storms](unit5-storm-paths.qmd) chapters you figured out a lot about winter storms. But the class still has open questions about **hurricanes**.

Just as we studied one winter storm (Jonas) to explain winter storms in general, we now study **one hurricane season** to explain hurricanes in general.

**Investigative phenomenon:** In 2005, hurricanes occurred in the North Atlantic Ocean between **June and November 30**, just like in 2018 and 2020.
:::

In class you watched the **2005 Hurricane Season** video (1:42–3:45). In that animation, ocean color shows **sea surface temperature**: red is warmest, blue is coldest. Below is every named storm of that record-breaking season, placed on the calendar by the date it formed.

      ]

      Plot.ruleY([0])
    ]

}

<p class="hu-note">Data: NOAA National Hurricane Center Tropical Cyclone Reports for 2005 (formation dates approximate to a day). 2005 had 27 named storms (plus one unnamed subtropical storm), 15 hurricanes, 7 major hurricanes, and 4 Category 5s: Emily, Katrina, Rita and Wilma. Zeta formed on December 30, after the official season.</p>

::: {.student-task}
### ✏️ In your packet: initial ideas (Rumors)

Jot down your ideas for: **What caused the patterns of location and time of year we observed from the 2005 hurricane season over the North Atlantic Ocean?** Sentence starters:

- *Hurricanes form near the equator and die after moving north as a result of… I think this because…*
- *Hurricanes form between June and November as a result of… I think this because…*

In class, the **Rumors** routine had you trade ideas about what causes a hurricane to form and what makes it stronger. On your own, write down your idea plus one different idea a classmate might have.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 🔑 Check your thinking (try it first!)

Ideas students often come up with (you will test them in this chapter):

- Hurricanes form near the equator because the **water is warmer**, and die after moving north because the **water is cooler**. Evidence: in the video, storms formed where the water was red and weakened where it was yellow or blue.
- Hurricanes occur between June and November because it is **warmer** then, so the **water is warmer**.

It's fine if your ideas are incomplete. You will refine them with data.
:::

# Explore: What Patterns Do We See in Global Occurrence of Hurricanes? {#hu-explore}

::: {.explore-box}
## 🔬 Where, how many, and when?

Hurricanes are one kind of **tropical cyclone**. In the Northwest Pacific they're called **typhoons**, and in the Indian Ocean and South Pacific, **cyclones**. Same storm, different names. You'll look for patterns in **where**, **how many**, and **when**, and then compare them to **where the warm water is**.
:::

## Where do hurricanes happen? {#hu-where}

There are **six regions** of the world where hurricanes (tropical cyclones) are likely to occur. Your packet's map ("Where do tropical cyclones take place?", BBC/NOAA) shows every historic storm track from 1842–2023. The map below outlines the same six regions. Tap a region name to learn about it.

      ...huRegions.map(g => Plot.line(huRing(g.box), {stroke: huHemiColor[g.hemi], strokeWidth: g.name === huPick ? 4 : 1.8, strokeDasharray: g.name === huPick ? null : "6,3",
        fill: huHemiColor[g.hemi], fillOpacity: g.name === huPick ? 0.18 : 0.06})),
      Plot.text(huRegions, {x: d => d.label[0], y: d => d.label[1], text: "name", fontWeight: "bold", fontSize: width < 500 ? 9 : 12,
        fill: d => huHemiColor[d.hemi], stroke: "white", strokeWidth: 3}),
      Plot.text([{x: 205, y: 2}], {x: "x", y: "y", text: () => "Equator", fontSize: 10, fill: "#334155", textAnchor: "start", dy: -6})
    ]
  });
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const r = huRegions.find(d => d.name === huPick);
  return html`<div class="hu-card"><b>${r.name}</b> (${r.hemi} Hemisphere)<br>
    Hurricane season: <b>${r.season}</b> · Average hurricanes per year: <b>${r.avg}</b><br>
    <span style="font-size:.9em;">Location: about ${Math.abs(r.box[0][1])}°–${Math.abs(r.box[1][1])}° ${r.hemi === "Northern" ? "N" : "S"} of the equator. Notice the region starts a few degrees away from the equator, not right on it.</span></div>`;
}
```

<p class="hu-note">Region outlines are approximate, drawn to match the packet map. Blue = Northern Hemisphere regions, red = Southern Hemisphere regions. A strip right along the equator has almost no storms: there, Earth's spin can't start air spinning (the Coriolis effect is zero at the equator).</p>

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
huQuiz("hu-q-where", "Check: where do hurricanes happen?", [
  {q: "What pattern do you see in where tropical cyclones take place?",
   options: ["Mostly near the poles", "In bands over tropical oceans on both sides of the equator, but not right on it", "Only in the Atlantic Ocean", "Over the middle of continents"],
   correct: 1,
   explanation: "All six regions are over oceans in the tropics, roughly 5°–30° from the equator, in both hemispheres. None is over land or near the poles."},
  {q: "Which region is closest to New York City?",
   options: ["East Pacific", "North Atlantic", "North Indian", "Southwest Pacific"],
   correct: 1,
   explanation: "NYC sits on the northern edge of the North Atlantic region. Storms like Sandy (2012), Irene (2011) and Henri (2021) came from there."}
])
```

## How many hurricanes happen? {#hu-how-many}

The number of hurricanes (strong tropical cyclones) varies a bit from year to year, but the **average** tells you how many are likely. This is the packet's NOAA data table, made into the bar graph your packet asks for.

| Hurricane Region | Hurricane Season | Number of Hurricanes per Year (average) |
|---|---|---|
| East Pacific Ocean | May–November | 9 |
| West Pacific Ocean | April–January | 16 |
| North Atlantic | June–November | 7 |
| Southwestern Pacific | October–May | 4 |
| North Indian Ocean | April–December | 2 |
| South Indian Ocean | October–May | 6 |

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof huBarSort = Inputs.radio(["Packet order", "Most to fewest"], {value: "Packet order", label: "Order:"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const order = ["East Pacific", "West Pacific", "North Atlantic", "North Indian", "Southwest Pacific", "South Indian"];
  const dom = huBarSort === "Packet order" ? order : [...huRegions].sort((a, b) => b.avg - a.avg).map(d => d.name);
  return Plot.plot({
    title: "Average number of hurricanes (tropical cyclones) in a year",
    subtitle: "Blue = Northern Hemisphere, red = Southern Hemisphere. Source: NOAA (packet table).",
    width, height: 320, marginLeft: 40, marginBottom: 50,
    x: {domain: dom, label: null, tickFormat: d => width < 520 ? d.replace("Southwest", "SW").replace("North ", "N. ").replace("South ", "S. ").replace("East ", "E. ").replace("West ", "W. ") : d},
    y: {domain: [0, 20], label: "Hurricanes per year", grid: true},
    marks: [
      Plot.barY(huRegions, {x: "name", y: "avg", fill: d => huHemiColor[d.hemi]}),
      Plot.text(huRegions, {x: "name", y: "avg", text: d => String(d.avg), dy: -8, fontWeight: "bold"}),
      Plot.ruleY([0])
    ]
  });
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
huQuiz("hu-q-howmany", "Check: how many hurricanes?", [
  {q: "Do all regions get the same number of hurricanes?",
   options: ["Yes, about 7 each", "No: the West Pacific averages 16 a year, eight times the North Indian Ocean's 2", "No: the North Atlantic has the most", "We can't tell from the table"],
   correct: 1,
   explanation: "The West Pacific is the busiest region on Earth. The North Atlantic (7 per year) is in the middle."},
  {q: "About how many hurricanes form worldwide in an average year, using the table?",
   options: ["About 7", "About 16", "About 44", "About 100"],
   correct: 2,
   explanation: "9 + 16 + 7 + 4 + 2 + 6 = 44. That matches the long-term global average of roughly 40–50 hurricanes a year."}
])
```

## When do hurricanes happen? {#hu-when}

**Hurricane season** is the time of year when hurricanes will most likely happen. But hurricane season is not at the same time in all places. Here is the packet's season calendar, filled in from the table.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof huGroup = Inputs.toggle({label: "Color the regions by hemisphere", value: false})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const order = ["East Pacific", "West Pacific", "North Atlantic", "North Indian", "Southwest Pacific", "South Indian"];
  const cells = huRegions.flatMap(r => r.months.map(m => ({region: r.name, month: huMonths[m], hemi: r.hemi})));
  return Plot.plot({
    title: "Hurricane season in each region",
    subtitle: huGroup ? "Blue = Northern Hemisphere, red = Southern Hemisphere" : "Shaded months = hurricane season",
    width, height: 280, marginLeft: width < 500 ? 104 : 130, marginBottom: 30,
    x: {domain: huMonths, label: null, axis: "top", tickFormat: d => width < 500 ? d[0] : d},
    y: {domain: order, label: null},
    marks: [
      Plot.cell(huRegions.flatMap(r => huMonths.map(m => ({region: r.name, month: m}))), {x: "month", y: "region", fill: "#f1f5f9", stroke: "#cbd5e1", inset: 1}),
      Plot.cell(cells, {x: "month", y: "region", fill: d => huGroup ? huHemiColor[d.hemi] : "#0f766e", inset: 1, title: d => `${d.region}: ${d.month}`})
    ]
  });
}
```

<p class="hu-note">From the packet's NOAA table. The North Atlantic's official season is June 1 – November 30, with a statistical peak around <b>September 10</b>.</p>

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
huQuiz("hu-q-when", "Check: when do hurricanes happen?", [
  {q: "The regions fall into two groups by timing. Which grouping is correct?",
   options: ["East Pacific, West Pacific, North Atlantic, North Indian (about April–November) vs. Southwest Pacific and South Indian (about October–May)", "North Atlantic alone vs. everyone else", "Pacific regions vs. Indian Ocean regions", "There is no pattern"],
   correct: 0,
   explanation: "Four regions peak in the middle of the calendar year; two peak around the turn of the year."},
  {q: "What do the regions in each group have in common? (Hint: the equator!)",
   options: ["They are all in the same ocean", "Each group is on the same side of the equator: Northern Hemisphere vs. Southern Hemisphere", "They all touch the United States", "They are the same size"],
   correct: 1,
   explanation: "The four mid-year regions are north of the equator; Southwest Pacific and South Indian are south of it."},
  {q: "Seasons are opposite in the two hemispheres. In which season are hurricanes most common?",
   options: ["Winter in each hemisphere", "Summer and early fall in each hemisphere", "Spring only", "All seasons equally"],
   correct: 1,
   explanation: "Northern regions: June–November is northern summer/fall. Southern regions: October–May covers southern summer (December–February) and early fall."}
])
```

:::

## Where's the warm water? {#hu-warm-water}

The temperature of the ocean surface is not the same everywhere, and it affects hurricanes. Your packet uses the **IRI Ocean Temperature** model from Columbia University's Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory and International Research Institute for Climate and Society, right here in New York City. The map below uses **the same data source**: NOAA's ERSST v5 sea surface temperatures, averaged for each month over 1991–2020 and downloaded from the IRI Data Library.

Choose a month (or a 3-month season). Then turn on **Only show water ≥ 26.5 °C** to color just the warmest water, like the packet's red/orange pencil step.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false

//| echo: false
huSst = {
  const A = "0123456789ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZabcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz!#$%&()*+-";
  return huSstRaw.map(s => Array.from(s, ch => ch === "." ? null : A.indexOf(ch) / 2 - 2));
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
huCells = {
  const out = [];
  for (let i = 0; i < 21; i++) for (let j = 0; j < 60; j++) {
    const lat = -40 + 4 * i, lon = 6 * j;
    const y0 = lat - 2, y1 = lat + 2, x0 = lon - 3, x1 = lon + 3;
    out.push({k: i * 60 + j, lat, lon, geom: {type: "Polygon", coordinates: [[[x0, y0], [x0, y1], [x1, y1], [x1, y0], [x0, y0]]]}});
  }
  return out;
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
huSstFor = (sel, offset = 0) => {
  const idx = sel.startsWith("Jun") ? [5, 6, 7] : sel.startsWith("Dec") ? [11, 0, 1] : [huMonths.indexOf(sel)];
  return huCells.map(c => {
    const v = idx.map(m => huSst[m][c.k]);
    return v.some(x => x === null) ? null : d3.mean(v) + offset;
  });
}
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
huSstMap = (sel, opts, offset = 0, title) => {
  const vals = huSstFor(sel, offset);
  const hot = opts.includes("Only show water ≥ 26.5 °C");
  const showReg = opts.includes("Show the six hurricane regions");
  const data = huCells.map((c, i) => ({...c, t: vals[i]})).filter(d => d.t !== null);
  const color = hot
    ? {type: "threshold", domain: [26.5, 28, 29, 30], range: ["#e2e8f0", "#fdba74", "#f97316", "#dc2626", "#7f1d1d"], legend: true, label: "Sea surface temperature (°C)", tickFormat: d => d}
    : {type: "threshold", domain: [5, 10, 15, 20, 24, 26.5, 28, 30], range: ["#312e81", "#1d4ed8", "#0ea5e9", "#5eead4", "#bbf7d0", "#fde68a", "#fb923c", "#dc2626", "#7f1d1d"], legend: true, label: "Sea surface temperature (°C)", tickFormat: d => d};
  return Plot.plot({
    title: title || `Sea surface temperature: ${sel}`,
    width, height: Math.round(width * 0.42), projection: huProj, color,
    marks: [
      Plot.sphere({fill: "#e5e7eb"}),
      Plot.geo(data, {geometry: "geom", fill: "t"}),
      huLand ? Plot.geo(huLand, {fill: "#9ca3af", stroke: "#4b5563", strokeWidth: 0.4}) : null,
      Plot.line(d3.range(0, 361, 5).map(x => [x, 0]), {stroke: "#111827", strokeDasharray: "5,4", strokeWidth: 1}),
      ...(showReg ? huRegions.map(g => Plot.line(huRing(g.box), {stroke: "#111827", strokeWidth: 1.6, strokeDasharray: "6,3"})) : []),
      showReg ? Plot.text(huRegions, {x: d => d.label[0], y: d => d.label[1], text: "name", fontSize: width < 500 ? 8 : 11, fontWeight: "bold", fill: "#111827", stroke: "white", strokeWidth: 3}) : null,
      Plot.tip(data, Plot.pointer({x: "lon", y: "lat", title: d => `${Math.abs(d.lat)}°${d.lat >= 0 ? "N" : "S"}, ${d.lon <= 180 ? d.lon + "°E" : (360 - d.lon) + "°W"}\n${d.t.toFixed(1)} °C`}))
    ]
  });
}
```

## See-Think-Wonder {#hu-stw}

::: {.student-task}
### ✏️ In your packet: See-Think-Wonder

Complete 2–3 rows: **What patterns do you see in the location of tropical cyclones? In the time of year they occur? In sea surface temperature throughout any given year?** Then: **How does the warm water during the Northern Hemisphere's summer and winter relate to the times of year that hurricanes occur most frequently in different regions?**
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 🔑 Check your thinking (try it first!)

The key observations (you'll need these in Explain):

- Tropical cyclones occur **near the equator in both the Northern and Southern Hemispheres**.
- Tropical cyclones occur during the **warmer months in each hemisphere**.
- Sea temperature follows air temperature and the seasons in each hemisphere.
- Tropical cyclones occur at the **locations and times of year when air and sea temperatures are warmest**.

Good "wonder" questions: *Why* do tropical cyclones occur when the air and sea are warmer? Does heat give tropical cyclones their energy?

**About the model:** the IRI maps come from a computational model that combines many data sets. Every model makes assumptions and approximations. Keep that in mind; you'll come back to it in Evaluate.
:::

# Explain: What Explains Patterns of Hurricane Occurrence? {#hu-explain}

::: {.explain-box}
## ⚡ What does a hurricane need to form and gain strength?

In class you watched **How Do Hurricanes Happen** (only up to 1:17, because the rest gives away predictions you'll make yourself) and analyzed the **Hurricane Formation Diagram**. The diagram's steps:

1. **#1** Warm ocean water (more than 80 °F) provides energy for the hurricane and causes more evaporation, making humid air and clouds.
2. **#2** Winds coming together force air upward.
3. **#3** Winds flow outward above the storm, allowing the air below to rise.
4. **#4** Humid air rising makes the clouds of the storm.
5. **#5** Light winds outside the hurricane steer it and let it grow.

**Energy source:** warm water. As water vapor **evaporates** it carries heat energy into the atmosphere. Then water vapor **condenses, releasing the heat energy**. Rising air spirals, creating the **eye** (a low-pressure zone).
:::

## Part 1: Hurricane Model Illustrating What is Happening to Water Molecules {#hu-explain-1}

Your packet asks you to **revise the diagram to show what is happening to the ocean water on a molecular scale**: what causes the water to rise up and form clouds? Use this virtual model to see it. Each dot is a (very!) simplified water molecule.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
huMolecules = {
  const W = Math.min(width, 680), H = 380;
  const wrap = html`<div style="max-width:${W}px;margin:0 auto;">
    <div style="display:flex;flex-wrap:wrap;gap:10px;align-items:center;margin-bottom:8px;">
      <label style="font-weight:700;">Ocean surface temperature: <span class="hu-tlab">27.0</span> °C</label>
      <input class="hu-trange" type="range" min="20" max="31" step="0.5" value="27" style="flex:1 1 180px;min-height:36px;" aria-label="Ocean surface temperature">
      <button class="hu-btn hu-pause" type="button">⏸ Pause</button>
    </div>
    <canvas style="width:100%;height:auto;border-radius:12px;display:block;" role="img" aria-label="Animated model: water molecules evaporate from warm ocean, rise, condense into cloud and release heat"></canvas>
    <div class="hu-readout" style="display:flex;flex-wrap:wrap;gap:8px;margin-top:8px;"></div>
  </div>`;
  const canvas = wrap.querySelector("canvas");
  const dpr = window.devicePixelRatio || 1;
  canvas.width = W * dpr; canvas.height = H * dpr;
  const ctx = canvas.getContext("2d"); ctx.scale(dpr, dpr);
  const range = wrap.querySelector(".hu-trange"), tlab = wrap.querySelector(".hu-tlab");
  const readout = wrap.querySelector(".hu-readout");
  const pauseBtn = wrap.querySelector(".hu-pause");
  let T = 27, paused = false;
  range.oninput = () => { T = +range.value; tlab.textContent = T.toFixed(1); };
  pauseBtn.onclick = () => { paused = !paused; pauseBtn.textContent = paused ? "▶ Play" : "⏸ Pause"; };
  const es = t => 6.112 * Math.exp(17.67 * t / (t + 243.5));     // saturation vapor pressure (hPa)
  const seaY = H * 0.72, condY = H * 0.30;
  const liquid = d3.range(90).map(() => ({x: Math.random() * W, y: seaY + 8 + Math.random() * (H - seaY - 14), ph: Math.random() * 6.28}));
  let vapor = [], cloud = [], flashes = [], condTimes = [], frame = 0;
  function draw() {
    if (!paused) {
      frame++;
      const ratio = es(T) / es(26.5);
      // evaporation: chance per frame grows with saturation vapor pressure (more fast molecules escape)
      if (Math.random() < 0.16 * ratio ** 2.2) {
        vapor.push({x: 30 + Math.random() * (W - 60), y: seaY - 2, vy: -(0.55 + 0.05 * (T - 20)), hot: true});
      }
      vapor.forEach(v => {
        v.y += v.vy * (1 + 0.15 * (seaY - v.y) / seaY);
        const dx = W / 2 - v.x;                                    // #2 winds come together
        v.x += Math.sign(dx) * Math.min(Math.abs(dx), 0.35) * (v.y < seaY - 40 ? 1 : 0.3);
      });
      vapor.filter(v => v.y <= condY).forEach(v => {
        cloud.push({x: v.x + (Math.random() - 0.5) * 70, y: condY - 10 - Math.random() * 50, r: 6 + Math.random() * 9, life: 420});
        flashes.push({x: v.x, y: condY, life: 30});
        condTimes.push(frame);
      });
      vapor = vapor.filter(v => v.y > condY);
      cloud.forEach(c => { c.life--; c.x += (c.x - W / 2) * 0.002; });   // #3 outflow aloft
      cloud = cloud.filter(c => c.life > 0).slice(-160);
      flashes.forEach(f => f.life--); flashes = flashes.filter(f => f.life > 0);
      condTimes = condTimes.filter(t => frame - t < 300);
    }
    // sky
    const g = ctx.createLinearGradient(0, 0, 0, seaY);
    g.addColorStop(0, "#1e293b"); g.addColorStop(1, "#64748b");
    ctx.fillStyle = g; ctx.fillRect(0, 0, W, seaY);
    // ocean (color by temperature)
    ctx.fillStyle = d3.interpolateRgb("#1d4ed8", "#ea580c")((T - 20) / 11);
    ctx.fillRect(0, seaY, W, H - seaY);
    // condensation level
    ctx.setLineDash([6, 5]); ctx.strokeStyle = "rgba(255,255,255,.5)"; ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(0, condY); ctx.lineTo(W, condY); ctx.stroke(); ctx.setLineDash([]);
    ctx.fillStyle = "#e2e8f0"; ctx.font = "12px Inter, sans-serif";
    ctx.fillText("Air cools as it rises → water vapor condenses here", 8, condY + 15);
    // clouds
    cloud.forEach(c => { ctx.fillStyle = `rgba(241,245,249,${Math.min(1, c.life / 120) * 0.85})`; ctx.beginPath(); ctx.arc(c.x, c.y, c.r, 0, 6.283); ctx.fill(); });
    // heat flashes
    flashes.forEach(f => { ctx.strokeStyle = `rgba(250,204,21,${f.life / 30})`; ctx.lineWidth = 2; ctx.beginPath(); ctx.arc(f.x, f.y, 34 - f.life, 0, 6.283); ctx.stroke(); });
    ctx.lineWidth = 1;
    // vapor molecules
    vapor.forEach(v => { ctx.fillStyle = "#fb923c"; ctx.beginPath(); ctx.arc(v.x, v.y, 3.6, 0, 6.283); ctx.fill(); });
    // liquid molecules (jiggle more when warmer)
    const amp = 0.6 + (T - 20) * 0.22;
    liquid.forEach(m => { m.ph += 0.08 + (T - 20) * 0.02;
      ctx.fillStyle = "rgba(224,242,254,.85)"; ctx.beginPath(); ctx.arc(m.x + Math.cos(m.ph) * amp, m.y + Math.sin(m.ph * 1.3) * amp, 3, 0, 6.283); ctx.fill(); });
    ctx.fillStyle = "#fff"; ctx.font = "bold 13px Inter, sans-serif";
    ctx.fillText(`Warm ocean: ${T.toFixed(1)} °C (${(T * 9 / 5 + 32).toFixed(0)} °F)`, 8, H - 10);
    ctx.font = "12px Inter, sans-serif";
    ctx.fillText("● orange = water vapor carrying heat energy up", 8, seaY - 10);
    // readout
    if (frame % 15 === 0 || paused) {
      const grow = T >= 26.5;
      readout.innerHTML = `
        <div class="hu-card" style="flex:1 1 150px;margin:0;"><b>Evaporation</b><br>${Math.round(100 * (es(T) / es(26.5)) ** 2.2)}% of the rate at 26.5 °C</div>
        <div class="hu-card" style="flex:1 1 150px;margin:0;"><b>Water vapor air can hold</b><br>${(es(T) / es(26.5) * 100).toFixed(0)}% of 26.5 °C air</div>
        <div class="hu-card" style="flex:1 1 180px;margin:0;background:${grow ? "#fee2e2" : "#e0f2fe"};"><b>Storm energy</b><br>${grow ? "▲ Heat released by condensation is more than the storm loses: the storm can form and strengthen" : "▼ Not enough heat released: the storm can't form or it weakens"}</div>`;
    }
    raf = requestAnimationFrame(draw);
  }
  let raf = requestAnimationFrame(draw);
  invalidation.then(() => cancelAnimationFrame(raf));
  return wrap;
}
```

<p class="hu-note">A simplified model. Evaporation and the amount of water vapor air can hold both grow with temperature (about 6–7% more per °C). The "storm energy" box uses the observed rule of thumb that hurricanes need water of about 26.5 °C or warmer; real storms also need moist air, low wind shear and some spin from Earth's rotation.</p>

**What the model shows, molecule by molecule:**

| Step | What the molecules are doing | Energy |
|---|---|---|
| Warm water | Water molecules move faster when warmer. The fastest ones at the surface break free (**evaporation**). | Thermal energy from the ocean becomes **latent heat** stored in the vapor |
| Moist air rises | Warm, humid air is **less dense** than the cooler air around it, so it rises. Winds coming together push it up. | Vapor carries the energy upward |
| Clouds form | Rising air cools; slower vapor molecules stick together into droplets (**condensation**). | The latent heat is **released**, warming the air |
| Storm grows | Warmed air rises even faster, lowering the air pressure at the surface, so more air rushes in and spirals. | Released heat → kinetic energy of wind |

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 🔑 Sample scientific explanation (try yours first!)

**Question:** What causes hurricane occurrence near the equator between June 1 and November 30?

**Claim:** Hurricanes occur near the equator from June 1 to November 30 because that is where and when the Northern Hemisphere's ocean water (and the air above it) is warmest, warm enough (about 26.5 °C / 80 °F or more) to supply the energy hurricanes need.

**Evidence:** The SST maps show water ≥ 26.5 °C in a belt near the equator, right where the six hurricane regions are. In the North Atlantic the water first reaches 26.5 °C around May–June and is warmest in September, matching the June–November season and the 2005 storms (most formed July–October). Southern Hemisphere regions have their season (October–May) when *their* water is warmest.

**Science concepts:** Warmer water has more fast-moving molecules, so more water evaporates. Warm, moist air is less dense, so it rises. As it rises it cools and the vapor condenses, releasing latent heat that makes the air rise faster and the winds stronger.

**Reasoning:** Because warm water causes more evaporation, it supplies more water vapor to rise and condense. Therefore enough energy is released for hurricanes to form and strengthen only where and when the water is warmest. When hurricanes move north over cooler water, not enough water evaporates, so they lose their energy and die.
:::

# Elaborate: What is happening to precipitation as global temperatures rise? {#hu-elaborate}

::: {.elaborate-box}
## 🌧️ The hidden danger: rain

So far we've focused on how often hurricanes form and how strong their **winds** are. In class you watched *More than 100 dead in devastation and flooding after Hurricane Helene* (0–1:50). Most of the deaths were caused by **water**, not wind.
:::

**From the packet's article (modified from NPR):**

- Hurricane **Helene** (2024) reached **Category 4**, but some of the worst damage was **hundreds of miles inland**. Around Asheville, N.C., **more than 15 inches** of rain fell on mountains already soaked from earlier storms. The French Broad River crumbled highways, flooded homes and cut off drinking water.
- The heaviest storms in the southeastern U.S. are already dropping **37% more rain** than in 1958. As the climate keeps changing, that could increase by **20% or more**.
- The **Category** is based **entirely on wind speed**. Hurricane **Florence** (2018) hit North Carolina as only a **Category 1**, but the slow-moving storm dropped **up to 30 inches** of rain.

| Saffir-Simpson category | Sustained wind (mph) | What it *doesn't* tell you |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 74–95 | Rainfall |
| 2 | 96–110 | Storm surge height |
| 3 (major) | 111–129 | How slowly the storm moves |
| 4 (major) | 130–156 | How big the storm is |
| 5 (major) | 157 or higher | Flooding far inland |

The packet's map shows how much more rain now falls on the **heaviest 1% of days** in each U.S. region (1958–2021):

]

Why does warmer air mean more rain in a storm? Warmer air can **hold more water vapor**: about **7% more for each 1 °C** of warming. Try it:

```{ojs}
//| echo: false

```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const es = t => 6.112 * Math.exp(17.67 * t / (t + 243.5));
  const base = 28, pct = (es(base + huWarm) / es(base) - 1) * 100;
  const rows = [{k: "Today (28 °C)", v: 100}, {k: `Warmer (${(base + huWarm).toFixed(1)} °C)`, v: 100 + pct}];
  return html`<div>${Plot.plot({
    width: Math.min(width, 560), height: 150, marginLeft: 120, x: {domain: [0, 140], label: "Water vapor the air can hold (% of today)"}, y: {label: null},
    marks: [Plot.barX(rows, {y: "k", x: "v", fill: (d, i) => i ? "#2563eb" : "#93c5fd"}), Plot.text(rows, {y: "k", x: "v", text: d => d.v.toFixed(0) + "%", dx: 18, fontWeight: "bold"})]
  })}<div class="hu-card">+${huWarm} °C → about <b>${pct.toFixed(0)}% more</b> water vapor. More vapor feeding a storm means more condensation: <b>heavier rain</b> and more latent heat released.</div></div>`;
}
```

<p class="hu-note">Calculated with the Clausius-Clapeyron relationship (saturation vapor pressure of water). The IPCC (AR6) finds heavy rainfall gets about 7% more intense for each 1 °C of global warming.</p>

1. Rainfall in the heaviest storms has increased, for example 37% more in the Southeast since 1958; storms like Helene and Florence dropped 15–30 inches.
2. The Category only measures wind speed. Rain, flooding and storm surge cause much of the damage, even from "weak" storms.
3. Flooding far from the coast: destroyed highways and homes, lost drinking water and deaths (North Carolina); more rain on the heaviest days in most regions, +60% in the Northeast.
4. Higher temperatures warm the ocean, so more water evaporates (molecules gain energy). Warmer air can hold more water vapor (about 7% per °C). When that vapor rises and condenses in the storm, more rain falls (and more latent heat is released). So as global temperatures rise, tropical storms can drop more rain.

# Evaluate: What is the Future of Tropical Cyclones? {#hu-evaluate}

::: {.evaluate-box}
## 🔮 More frequent? More intense?

Your final task is to write an argument about whether hurricanes will become **more frequent** and/or **more intense** as global temperatures rise. First, collect the data you'll need.
:::

## Part 1: Is global warming affecting hurricanes? {#hu-trends}

Hurricanes form above warm ocean water, and warmer water may lead to stronger hurricanes. Earth warmed about 1 °F over the 20th century, and sea surface temperatures are climbing. Has that affected hurricanes? This is an area of active research. One way scientists study it is by looking at the **history of hurricanes**.

### Total number of hurricanes in different regions

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// Read from the packet graph (Klotzbach et al. 2022, Geophysical Research Letters). Stacked tops for each year in this order:
// South Pacific, South Indian, North Indian, western North Pacific, eastern North Pacific, North Atlantic. Accurate to about ±1.
huTotalsRaw = [
  [1990,5,12,13,34,50,58],[1991,4,12,13,33,43,47],[1992,9,15,18,39,55,59],[1993,6,12,14,34,45,49],[1994,3,17,18,38,48,51],
  [1995,3,14,16,31,38,49],[1996,4,18,22,43,48,57],[1997,12,21,23,46,55,58],[1998,9,17,22,31,40,50],[1999,2,11,14,25,31,39],
  [2000,4,15,17,31,37,45],[2001,3,12,13,34,42,51],[2002,2,13,13,29,37,41],[2003,6,18,19,36,43,50],[2004,2,12,14,34,40,49],
  [2005,6,11,11,29,36,51],[2006,7,12,13,26,37,42],[2007,4,15,18,34,38,44],[2008,2,12,13,25,32,40],[2009,2,11,12,27,35,38],
  [2010,6,12,15,24,27,39],[2011,5,11,12,22,32,39],[2012,3,12,12,27,37,47],[2013,3,15,19,35,44,46],[2014,3,10,12,24,40,46],
  [2015,6,12,14,34,50,54],[2016,4,9,10,27,40,47],[2017,4,9,11,24,33,43],[2018,5,18,22,38,51,59],[2019,5,18,24,42,49,55],
  [2020,5,12,16,28,32,46],[2021,4,9,12,22,30,37]
]
huBasinNames = ["South Pacific", "South Indian", "North Indian", "Western North Pacific", "Eastern North Pacific", "North Atlantic"]
huBasinCols = ["#0b1f4d", "#1d4ed8", "#38bdf8", "#5eead4", "#bef264", "#fef9c3"]
huTotals = huTotalsRaw.flatMap(([year, ...c]) => c.map((v, i) => ({year, basin: huBasinNames[i], n: v - (i ? c[i - 1] : 0)})))
huFit = (pts) => {
  const mx = d3.mean(pts, d => d.x), my = d3.mean(pts, d => d.y);
  let a = 0, b = 0; for (const p of pts) { a += (p.x - mx) * (p.y - my); b += (p.x - mx) ** 2; }
  const m = a / b; return {m, b: my - m * mx};
}
```

```{ojs}

viewof huBasinSel = Inputs.checkbox(huBasinNames, {value: huBasinNames, label: "Include:"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const sel = huTotals.filter(d => huBasinSel.includes(d.basin));
  const yr = d3.rollups(sel, v => d3.sum(v, d => d.n), d => d.year).map(([x, y]) => ({x, y}));
  if (!yr.length) return html`<p>Pick at least one region.</p>`;
  const f = huFit(yr);
  const line = [{year: 1990, v: f.m * 1990 + f.b}, {year: 2021, v: f.m * 2021 + f.b}];
  return html`<div>${Plot.plot({
    title: "Hurricanes per year in the selected regions, 1990–2021",
    subtitle: "Dashed = straight-line trend",
    width, height: 340, marginLeft: 40,
    x: {label: null, tickFormat: d => String(d), domain: d3.range(1990, 2022), ticks: d3.range(1990, 2022, 4), type: "band"},
    y: {label: "Hurricanes", grid: true},
    color: {domain: huBasinNames, range: huBasinCols, legend: true},
    marks: [
      Plot.barY(sel, {x: "year", y: "n", fill: "basin", stroke: "#475569", strokeWidth: 0.3, order: huBasinNames, tip: true, title: d => `${d.year} ${d.basin}: ${d.n}`}),
      Plot.line(line, {x: "year", y: "v", stroke: "currentColor", strokeDasharray: "6,4", strokeWidth: 2})
    ]
  })}<div class="hu-card">Trend: <b>${f.m >= 0 ? "+" : ""}${(f.m * 10).toFixed(1)} hurricanes per decade</b> (about ${Math.round(f.m * 1990 + f.b)} per year in 1990 → ${Math.round(f.m * 2021 + f.b)} in 2021). ${Math.abs(f.m * 10) < 0.5 ? "That's basically flat." : f.m < 0 ? "A slight decrease." : "A slight increase."}</div></div>`;
}

So the trend is **not the same everywhere**, and the North Atlantic, NYC's region, saw an increase.

## Part 2: Using Climate Models to Make Predictions About the Future {#hu-part2}

### Reviewing what we know about hurricane formation {#hu-review}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 🔑 1. What is required for a hurricane to form? 2. How does a hurricane gain more energy? (try it first!)

1. **Warm ocean water** (about 26.5 °C / 80 °F or warmer) that causes lots of evaporation; humid air; winds coming together at the surface that force air upward; winds flowing outward above the storm; and light winds outside the hurricane that let it grow (and enough distance from the equator for the storm to spin).
2. From **warm water**: water evaporates and carries heat energy into the atmosphere. When the vapor **condenses**, it **releases** that heat, warming the air so it rises faster; surface pressure drops and the winds strengthen. Warmer water → more evaporation → more energy released.
:::

### What do global climate models tell us about sea surface temperature where hurricanes form? {#hu-ipcc}

Your packet uses the **[IPCC WGI Interactive Atlas](https://interactive-atlas.ipcc.ch/)** (Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, Working Group I). Steps: choose **Season → Customized season** (for example June to November for the North Atlantic), click the regions where hurricanes form, then look at the line graph. Try variables like **mean temperature**, **sea surface temperature**, **maximum 1-day precipitation** and **surface wind speed**. The Atlas works best on a laptop.

Below is a quick **what-if model** using the real 1991–2020 sea surface temperatures from Explore. It adds the same warming everywhere, which is a big simplifying **assumption** (real models warm different places by different amounts).

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof huPlus = Inputs.range([0, 3], {step: 0.5, value: 0, label: "Ocean warming added (°C):"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof huPlusMonth = Inputs.select(["Jun–Aug (average)", "Dec–Feb (average)", ...huMonths], {label: "Month:", value: "Sep"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const v0 = huSstFor(huPlusMonth, 0), v1 = huSstFor(huPlusMonth, huPlus);
  const ocean = huCells.map((c, i) => ({c, a: v0[i], b: v1[i]})).filter(d => d.a !== null);
  const share = (k) => ocean.filter(d => d[k] >= 26.5).length / ocean.length * 100;
  const nyc = huSstFor(huPlusMonth, huPlus)[huCells.findIndex(c => c.lat === 40 && c.lon === 288)];
  return html`<div>${huSstMap(huPlusMonth, ["Only show water ≥ 26.5 °C", "Show the six hurricane regions"], huPlus, `What if the ocean were ${huPlus} °C warmer? (${huPlusMonth})`)}
  <div class="hu-card">Ocean between 40° S and 40° N that is ≥ 26.5 °C: <b>${share("a").toFixed(0)}%</b> today → <b>${share("b").toFixed(0)}%</b> with +${huPlus} °C. Water off New York (40° N, 72° W): <b>${nyc === null ? "n/a" : nyc.toFixed(1) + " °C"}</b>.</div></div>`;
}
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## ⚠️ Why "more warm water" doesn't automatically mean "more hurricanes"

The 26.5 °C rule of thumb works for **today's** climate. As the planet warms, the **air** warms too, so the temperature needed for storms to form is expected to **rise along with the ocean**. Climate models also project changes in wind shear and humidity. That's why the IPCC projects:

- **Frequency:** the global number of tropical cyclones will **decrease or stay about the same** (medium confidence). Confidence in past trends of frequency is **low**.
- **Intensity:** the **proportion of Category 4–5** storms and the peak winds of the strongest storms will **increase** (high confidence).
- **Rain:** rainfall rates will **increase** (high confidence), roughly in line with "7% more water vapor per °C."
:::

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
huQuiz("hu-q-ipcc", "Check: climate models", [
  {q: "In the what-if model, the area of ocean warmer than 26.5 °C grows as you add warming. What is the best conclusion?",
   options: ["Hurricanes will definitely double in number", "Warm water will cover more area, giving storms more energy, but more warm water alone doesn't prove more storms, because the formation threshold may also rise", "Hurricanes will stop forming", "Warming won't change the ocean"],
   correct: 1,
   explanation: "This is a reasoning trap. Energy available per storm rises (supporting more intensity and rain), but how many storms form depends on more than one threshold."},
  {q: "According to the IPCC, which change is most certain?",
   options: ["Many more hurricanes each year", "A larger proportion of very intense (Cat 4–5) storms and heavier rain", "Hurricanes reaching the North Pole", "Fewer intense storms"],
   correct: 1,
   explanation: "IPCC AR6: high confidence that the proportion of intense storms and rainfall rates increase with warming; frequency changes are less certain."}
])
```

### Reliability of Models Based on Assumptions {#hu-reliability}

| Idea | Meaning (packet's apple-scale example) |
|---|---|
| **Precision** | Gives consistent results: the scale shows 100 g every time for the same 100 g apple |
| **Reliability** | You can trust it to stay accurate over time and in different situations: different apple sizes, months later |
| **Assumptions** | The ideas a model is built on. Accurate assumptions → a more precise and reliable model |

The IPCC Atlas warming scenarios rest on assumptions about **greenhouse gas emissions**, **economic and population growth**, **technological changes**, **policy and mitigation**, **land use changes**, **climate feedbacks**, and **socioeconomic choices**. Different assumptions give different futures:

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
huSSP = [
  {name: "SSP1-1.9", story: "Very low emissions: net-zero CO₂ around 2050", t: 1.4, lo: 1.0, hi: 1.8},
  {name: "SSP1-2.6", story: "Low emissions: net-zero CO₂ after 2050", t: 1.8, lo: 1.3, hi: 2.4},
  {name: "SSP2-4.5", story: "Intermediate: emissions stay near today's until mid-century", t: 2.7, lo: 2.1, hi: 3.5},
  {name: "SSP3-7.0", story: "High: emissions double by 2100", t: 3.6, lo: 2.8, hi: 4.6},
  {name: "SSP5-8.5", story: "Very high: emissions double by 2050", t: 4.4, lo: 3.3, hi: 5.7}
]
```

```

  return html`<div>${Plot.plot({

    subtitle: "Dot = best estimate; bar = very likely range",
    width, height: 250, marginLeft: 80,
    x: {domain: [0, 6], label: "Warming (°C)", grid: true},
    y: {domain: huSSP.map(d => d.name), label: null},
    marks: [
      Plot.ruleY(huSSP, {y: "name", x1: "lo", x2: "hi", stroke: d => d.name === huSSPpick ? "#dc2626" : "#94a3b8", strokeWidth: 6}),
      Plot.dot(huSSP, {y: "name", x: "t", r: 6, fill: d => d.name === huSSPpick ? "#7f1d1d" : "#475569", stroke: "white"}),
      Plot.text(huSSP, {y: "name", x: "hi", text: d => d.t + " °C", dx: 22})
    ]
  })}<div class="hu-card"><b>${s.name}:</b> ${s.story}. Best estimate <b>+${s.t} °C</b> (very likely ${s.lo}–${s.hi} °C).</div></div>`;

    .attr("role", "img").attr("aria-label", "Flowchart of my hurricane model");

    .append("path").attr("d", "M0,0L10,5L0,10z").attr("fill", "#64748b");
  all.forEach((d, i) => {
    const y = i * (bh + gap);
    const fill = d.k === "out" ? "#fee2e2" : d.k === "limit" ? "#fef3c7" : d.micro ? "#ede9fe" : "#e0f2fe";
    svg.append("rect").attr("x", 10).attr("y", y).attr("width", bw).attr("height", bh).attr("rx", 10).attr("fill", fill).attr("stroke", "#64748b");
    const fo = svg.append("foreignObject").attr("x", 16).attr("y", y + 2).attr("width", bw - 12).attr("height", bh - 4);
    fo.append("xhtml:div").style("font", `600 ${bw < 400 ? 11.5 : 13}px Inter, sans-serif`).style("color", "#0f172a").style("height", (bh - 4) + "px")
      .style("display", "flex").style("align-items", "center").style("line-height", "1.2").text(d.t);
    if (i < n - 1) svg.append("line").attr("x1", 10 + bw / 2).attr("x2", 10 + bw / 2).attr("y1", y + bh).attr("y2", y + bh + gap - 2)
      .attr("stroke", "#64748b").attr("stroke-width", 2).attr("marker-end", "url(#hu-arrow)");
  });
  const micro = steps.filter(d => d.micro).length;
  return html`<div>${svg.node()}<div class="hu-card">${micro ? `✅ ${micro} small-scale mechanism(s) included.` : "⚠️ Add at least one 🔬 molecular-scale link: the PTO asks for small-scale mechanisms."} ${steps.some(d => d.k === "limit") ? "✅ Including limits will help your counterclaim." : "Tip: adding the 'Limits' box helps you think about a counterclaim."} Matter: water cycles from ocean → vapor → cloud → rain. Energy: ocean heat → latent heat → wind (kinetic energy).</div></div>`;
}
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 🔑 Sample argument for Task 2 (intensity), from the teacher guide's student work (try yours first!)

**IV:** global temperatures. **DV:** intensity of hurricanes.

*"In New York, where I live, hurricane intensity will likely increase as global temperatures rise. Hurricanes form when warm water evaporates, bringing high-energy molecules into the air. This energy fuels cyclones as air rushes in to fill the low-pressure zone caused by rising warm air. As temperatures rise, more energy is transferred to the air, causing stronger winds. Global temperatures are expected to rise, which will increase water temperatures and cause the energy transfer to the air to increase. As a result, hurricane intensity will increase. This prediction is corroborated by historical data, which shows the number of Category 4 and 5 storms increasing from 1990–2020."*

**To reach Proficient, add:** a counterclaim (for example, "Some evidence suggests storms near NYC may not get stronger, because the water off NYC stays below 26.5 °C and storms weaken before they arrive"), a rebuttal using the data, the specific numbers (North Atlantic Cat 4–5: 16 → 25), and an evaluation of the model (which IPCC scenario, and how assumptions limit reliability).

**For Task 1 (frequency)** the same student argued that frequency will increase, citing the NOAA map's North Atlantic increase. That's a defensible claim if you also handle the counterclaim: global totals haven't risen, and the IPCC projects global frequency to decrease or stay the same.
:::

# Chapter Summary

| Key Concept | Details |
|---|---|
| **Six hurricane regions** | East Pacific, West Pacific, North Atlantic, North Indian, South Indian, Southwest Pacific: tropical oceans in both hemispheres, but not right on the equator |
| **How many** | Average hurricanes per year: West Pacific 16, East Pacific 9, North Atlantic 7, South Indian 6, Southwest Pacific 4, North Indian 2 (about 44 worldwide) |
| **When** | Northern regions: about April/June–November; southern regions: October–May. Hurricanes happen in each hemisphere's summer and fall. Atlantic season June 1 – Nov 30, peak around Sep 10 |
| **Warm water** | Hurricanes need sea surface temperatures of about 26.5 °C (80 °F) or more; the warm belt follows the seasons; ocean temperatures peak in late summer |
| **Energy source** | Warm water evaporates (latent heat stored); warm moist air is less dense and rises; vapor condenses, releasing latent heat; air rises faster, pressure falls, winds strengthen |
| **Why they die** | Over cooler water or land, too little water evaporates to supply energy |
| **Variables** | IV: sea surface temperature (cause). DV: hurricane occurrence (effect) |
| **Rain** | Category = wind speed only. Warmer air holds about 7% more water vapor per °C → heavier rain (Northeast heavy-rain days +60% since 1958) |
| **Observed trends** | Global hurricane count about flat or slightly down since 1990 (North Atlantic up); Cat 4–5 storms and their share have increased |
| **Projections (IPCC AR6)** | Higher proportion of Cat 4–5 storms and higher rainfall rates (high confidence); global frequency decreases or stays the same (medium confidence) |
| **Models** | Predictions depend on assumptions (emissions, population, technology, policy); scenarios show a range: about 1.4–4.4 °C by 2100 |

<script>
(function() {
  var cards = [
    {text: "Hurricanes form right on the equator, where the water is warmest.", type: "Myth",
     explanation: "Almost no hurricanes form within about 5° of the equator. Storms need Earth's rotation to start spinning (the Coriolis effect), and that effect is zero at the equator."},
    {text: "A hurricane's main energy source is heat released when water vapor condenses into clouds.", type: "Fact",
     explanation: "Warm water evaporates, storing energy as latent heat. When the vapor condenses high in the storm, that heat is released, warming the air so it rises faster and strengthens the winds."},
    {text: "Hurricane season is at the same time of year everywhere in the world.", type: "Myth",
     explanation: "Seasons are opposite in the two hemispheres. Northern regions peak around June–November; the South Indian and Southwest Pacific regions peak around October–May."},
    {text: "The North Atlantic hurricane season peaks around September 10, not in July when the air is hottest.", type: "Fact",
     explanation: "Water has a high heat capacity, so the ocean warms slowly and reaches its highest temperatures in late summer, around September."},
    {text: "A Category 1 hurricane can't cause deadly flooding.", type: "Myth",
     explanation: "The Category measures only wind speed. Florence (2018) hit North Carolina as a Category 1 and dropped up to 30 inches of rain."},
    {text: "Warmer air can hold more water vapor, about 7% more for every 1 °C.", type: "Fact",
     explanation: "That's why heavy downpours, including hurricane rain, are getting heavier as Earth warms. The Northeast's heaviest rain days now drop about 60% more rain than in 1958."},
    {text: "Scientists are certain that global warming will make many more hurricanes form every year.", type: "Myth",
     explanation: "The IPCC projects global tropical cyclone frequency to decrease or stay about the same (medium confidence). The stronger evidence is for more intense storms and heavier rain."},
    {text: "The number of Category 4 and 5 storms increased in all six hurricane regions between 1975–1989 and 1990–2004.", type: "Fact",
     explanation: "Every region rose, from 171 to 269 in total (North Atlantic 16 → 25). The share of hurricanes reaching Cat 4–5 has also risen since 1990."}
  ];
  var idx = 0, score = 0, answered = 0, cardAnswered = false;
  function el(id) { return document.getElementById(id); }
  function updateCard() {
    if (idx >= cards.length) {
      ['humf-card','humf-myth','humf-fact','humf-feedback','humf-next'].forEach(function(i){ el(i).style.display = 'none'; });
      el('humf-done').style.display = 'block';
      el('humf-final').textContent = score;
      el('humf-count').textContent = cards.length;
      return;
    }
    el('humf-card').textContent = cards[idx].text;
    el('humf-progress').textContent = 'Card ' + (idx + 1) + ' of ' + cards.length;
    el('humf-feedback').style.display = 'none';
    el('humf-next').style.display = 'none';
    el('humf-myth').disabled = false; el('humf-fact').disabled = false;
    el('humf-myth').style.opacity = '1'; el('humf-fact').style.opacity = '1';
    cardAnswered = false;
  }
  window.humfAnswer = function(choice) {
    if (cardAnswered) return;
    cardAnswered = true; answered++;
    var card = cards[idx], correct = (choice === card.type);
    if (correct) score++;
    el('humf-score').textContent = score; el('humf-total').textContent = answered;
    var fb = el('humf-feedback');
    fb.style.display = 'block';
    fb.style.background = correct ? 'rgba(0,184,148,0.2)' : 'rgba(214,48,49,0.2)';
    fb.style.border = '1px solid ' + (correct ? '#00b894' : '#e17055');
    fb.innerHTML = '<strong>' + (correct ? '✅ Correct! ' : '❌ That\'s a ' + card.type + '! ') + '</strong>' + card.explanation;
    el('humf-myth').disabled = true; el('humf-fact').disabled = true;
    el('humf-myth').style.opacity = (choice === 'Myth') ? '1' : '0.5';
    el('humf-fact').style.opacity = (choice === 'Fact') ? '1' : '0.5';
    el('humf-next').style.display = 'block';
  };
  window.humfNext = function() { idx++; updateCard(); };
  window.humfRestart = function() {
    idx = 0; score = 0; answered = 0;
    el('humf-card').style.display = 'flex';
    el('humf-myth').style.display = 'block'; el('humf-fact').style.display = 'block';
    el('humf-done').style.display = 'none';
    el('humf-score').textContent = '0'; el('humf-total').textContent = '0';
    updateCard();
  };
  updateCard();
})();
</script>

//| echo: false
huEndQuiz = function(id, title, questions) {
  const outer = html`<div id="${id}" style="font-family:'Inter',sans-serif; max-width:720px; margin:18px auto;"></div>`;
  const header = html`<div style="background:linear-gradient(135deg,#0b5c8a 0%,#0a3d62 100%);color:#fff;border-radius:14px 14px 0 0;padding:18px 22px;">
    <div style="font-size:1.1em;font-weight:700;">📝 ${title}</div>
    <div style="font-size:0.85em;opacity:0.9;margin-top:4px;">Select an answer for each question. <span class="hu-score"></span></div>
  </div>`;
  const body = html`<div style="border:1.5px solid #bae6fd;border-top:none;border-radius:0 0 14px 14px;background:#f0f9ff;padding:14px;"></div>`;
  let nRight = 0, nDone = 0;
  const scoreEl = header.querySelector(".hu-score");
  huBuildCards(body, questions, ok => { nDone++; if (ok) nRight++; scoreEl.textContent = `Score: ${nRight} / ${nDone}`; });
  outer.appendChild(header);
  outer.appendChild(body);
  return outer;
}
```

   options: ["June–November", "October–May", "All year", "Only in July"],
   correct: 1,

  {q: "On the molecular scale, why does warm, moist air rise above the ocean?",
   options: ["Its molecules are moving faster and spread out, so the air is less dense than the cooler air around it", "Water molecules are heavier than air", "The eye pulls it up", "Cold air is less dense"],
   correct: 0,

  {q: "In the hurricane model, where is the stored energy actually released into the air?",

   correct: 1,
   explanation: "Evaporation takes energy from the ocean and stores it in the vapor; condensation releases it higher up, powering the storm."},
  {q: "A hurricane moves from 29 °C water near Florida to 21 °C water off New England. What most likely happens, and why?",
   options: ["It strengthens because cold water has more energy", "It weakens because less water evaporates, so less latent heat is released", "Nothing changes", "It turns into a tornado"],
   correct: 1,
   explanation: "This is the 'die after moving north' pattern from the 2005 video. Sandy (2012) stayed dangerous partly because it merged with a mid-latitude storm system, not because of warm water."},
  {q: "In the claim 'Higher sea surface temperatures cause more hurricanes to occur,' which is the dependent variable?",
   options: ["Sea surface temperature", "Hurricane occurrence", "The month", "The ocean"],
   correct: 1,
   explanation: "The dependent variable is the effect that responds: hurricane occurrence. SST is the independent variable (the cause)."},
  {q: "Hurricane Florence was a Category 1 at landfall but dropped up to 30 inches of rain. What does this show?",
   options: ["The Category measures wind speed only, not rain or flooding risk", "Category 1 storms are always the most dangerous", "Florence was misclassified", "Rain doesn't cause damage"],
   correct: 0,
   explanation: "Slow-moving storms in a warmer, wetter atmosphere can cause catastrophic flooding regardless of their wind category."},
  {q: "From 1990–2021 the total number of hurricanes stayed about the same or dipped slightly, while the share reaching Category 4–5 rose (about 35% → 42%). Which conclusion is best supported?",
   options: ["Hurricanes are becoming more frequent", "Hurricanes are becoming more intense, while frequency shows no clear increase", "Hurricanes are getting weaker", "Nothing has changed"],
   correct: 1,
   explanation: "Separate the two variables: frequency (how many) vs intensity (how strong). This data supports a rise in intensity, matching IPCC AR6."},
  {q: "A classmate argues: 'More of the ocean will be above 26.5 °C, so there will definitely be many more hurricanes.' What is the best counterclaim?",
   options: ["Warm water doesn't matter for hurricanes", "The air warms too, so the temperature needed to form storms may rise; wind shear and humidity also matter; IPCC projects global frequency to decrease or stay the same", "Hurricanes only form in winter", "There is no counterclaim"],
   correct: 1,
   explanation: "A strong counterclaim uses evidence and reasoning, not just disagreement. It also points to the limits of a simple model."},
  {q: "The IPCC shows end-of-century warming from about 1.4 °C (SSP1-1.9) to 4.4 °C (SSP5-8.5). Why give a range instead of one number?",
   options: ["The models don't work", "Future emissions depend on human choices (policy, technology, population), so each scenario is an 'if-then' prediction based on different assumptions", "Scientists can't agree on anything", "The range is a typo"],
   correct: 1,
   explanation: "Model predictions have limited precision and reliability because of their assumptions. A good argument names the scenario it uses."}
])
